chief_complaint: ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks a lingering stomach bug or flu he had recently has settled into his leg muscles and weakened them.
concerns: He is worried that the weakness will spread upward to his chest and stop him from being able to breathe.
expectations: He hopes to be admitted to the hospital right away for IV fluids and urgent treatment before his legs stop working entirely.

investigation_events.title: Emergency bedside respiratory measurements
investigation_events.availability_message: Bedside respiratory measurements are now available. Admission and serial monitoring should proceed immediately.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Guillain-Barre Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Guillain-Barre Syndrome: IVIG or Plasmapheresis, respiratory monitoring, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Guillain-Barre Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Transverse myelitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Respiratory or bulbar involvement.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes. HPI: Campylobacter infection, molecular mimicry.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Guillain-Barre Syndrome.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Guillain-Barre Syndrome.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently admit for neurology assessment and serial respiratory monitoring; use IVIG or plasmapheresis for clinically significant Guillain-Barre syndrome. Counsel the patient to seek immediate care for breathing or swallowing difficulty.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Guillain-Barre Syndrome

teaching.one_liner: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes, often after a Campylobacter infection triggering molecular mimicry.

must_ask.say: Did weakness start in the legs and move upward?
Any numbness along with the weakness?
How fast has this been worsening?

history.answer: My legs have become so weak over the last few days, and now the weakness is spreading up into my hands and arms.
I have both weakness and tingling. My legs give out when I try to stand, and my fingers and toes feel numb with pins and needles.
It is completely equal on both sides. It started in both feet and legs, and now it has spread symmetrically up into both hands and arms.
It started about four days ago, and before then I was completely normal and walking fine. It didn't happen in a single split second, but has built up day by day.
It has gotten noticeably worse every day, moving steadily upward from my feet to my legs and now to my upper body. Yesterday I started losing grip strength in both hands.
I can barely stand because my knees buckle under me, and I can't climb any stairs. Today I couldn't even button my shirt or hold my cup securely.
The weakness is constant all day and night and doesn't get better with rest. It doesn't start normal in the morning and wear down only after repeated use.
I have a dull, heavy ache in my lower back and thighs, but no sharp shooting pains down my legs. My neck doesn't hurt at all when I move it.
No, my face hasn't drooped, my speech isn't slurred, and I haven't had vision problems or room-spinning dizziness.
No, I have normal control over my bladder and bowels. The skin around my groin and buttocks feels completely normal as well.
My chest feels a bit tight and it's hard to take a deep breath when I lie flat. When I drank water earlier, it felt slightly awkward to swallow.
I haven't noticed any twitching under my skin or shrinking of my muscles. The muscles just feel completely limp and useless.
About two weeks ago, I had bad watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, and a mild fever after eating chicken. It lasted about four days and then fully resolved.
I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart problems. I've never been told I have a stroke risk.
I eat a balanced diet with plenty of meat and vegetables, and I've never had stomach surgery. I only drink a beer or two occasionally on weekends.
I don't take water pills, steroids, chemotherapy, or any other regular medications.
I work at an office desk, but I don't do repetitive heavy wrist straining or sit squatted for hours. This weakness is in both legs and arms entirely.
Both of my feet and hands have had a prickly, numb sensation like they are falling asleep. It started at my toes and has crept up to my ankles and wrists.
I thought maybe that bad stomach flu I had a couple of weeks ago never really left and is just attacking my muscles.
The weakness is moving up so fast that I'm terrified it will reach my chest and I won't be able to breathe.
I want to be admitted to the hospital immediately to get IV therapy before I lose the ability to stand at all.
I have always been healthy and have no history of chronic illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any prescription drugs, supplements, or herbal remedies.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink one or two beers socially once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife and our teenage son.
There is no family history of nerve disorders, paralysis, or autoimmune illnesses.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert, oriented male lying in bed in mild distress from anxiety; breathing is unlabored at rest but chest expansion appears mildly shallow.

Pupils equal and reactive to light, extraocular movements intact without ptosis, facial sensation and symmetrical movement intact, gag reflex present with mild bilateral palate weakness, and tongue midline.

Symmetric flaccid weakness: bilateral hip flexion 3/5, knee extension 3/5, ankle dorsiflexion 2/5, shoulder abduction 4/5, elbow flexion 4/5, and wrist extension 4/5; no muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
Mildly decreased pinprick and vibration sensation in a symmetric stocking-and-glove distribution up to the mid-shins and wrists, with preserved joint position sense.
Deep tendon reflexes are completely absent (0/4) bilaterally at the biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
Finger-to-nose coordination is intact without dysmetria, but unable to stand or perform heel-to-shin test due to marked bilateral lower extremity weakness.
No midline or paraspinal tenderness along the cervical, thoracic, or lumbar spine; straight-leg raise test is negative bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds throughout all lung fields bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
